title: The spread of elections
text:
Home Democracy

Most people around the world think democracy is a good way to run a country, but they are often dissatisfied with how it is working in practice and are concerned about where it is heading. 1

These worries are consistent with expert surveys tracking the state of democracy worldwide. Across measures of free and fair elections and other features of democracy, like civil rights and checks on power, dozens of countries have become less democratic over the last decade.

But if we step back and look at the longer history of democracy — as we’ll do in this article — we see a broader trend of remarkable progress. The world used to be deeply undemocratic, and despite setbacks, it remains much more democratic than it was only half a century ago.

That progress was never steady or secure. The rights and institutions that many of us now live under were built through many partial victories and outright setbacks.

We do not say this to dismiss the real issues that many democracies face today. Quite the opposite. The longer perspective helps us appreciate the democratic institutions that so many of us around the world continue to value, and the efforts that are necessary to protect and expand them.

That is the focus of this article. We look at how the building blocks of electoral democracy developed over the last two hundred years: how elections spread, voting rights expanded, and meaningful political competition developed.

# The spread of elections

In the late 18th century, political leaders were usually chosen by inheritance, force, or through negotiation among the elite. Many leaders were monarchs who inherited their position from their parents. Parliaments didn’t exist, or were similarly filled with aristocrats and bureaucrats.

Over the next two centuries, that changed. Most leaders in government and parliament are now elected. Some leaders still take power violently (usually through coups), but there are few monarchs left, and even fewer with political power. Most members of parliament, too, have to face elections.

The chart below tracks this rise in elections, using data from the Lexical Index project by political scientists Svend-Erik Skaaning, John Gerring, and Henrikas Bartusevičius. 2 We’ll use this source throughout the article.

The chart shows that barely any country had both an elected parliament and an elected government in the late 18th century. Only two of the 76 countries included did: the United Kingdom and the United States.

More countries began electing their leaders in the 19th and early 20th century, but it wasn’t until the second half of the 20th century that elections became the predominant way of choosing political leaders worldwide.

 Click to explore

Most recently, in 2025, only 34 countries didn’t have elected parliaments and governments; the other 165 did. You can see the breakdown in the small chart (click to enlarge).

With the previous chart, we also see that the spread of elections wasn’t stable. The world saw rapid progress in the aftermath of World War I, in the late 1950s and 1960s, and at the end of the 20th century. But elections declined during World War II and in the early 1970s.

Today, the number of countries with elected parliaments and governments is 165, down from an all-time high of 176 in 2016. In recent years, military coups and civil wars toppled elected governments and parliaments in countries like Afghanistan, Madagascar, Niger, and Sudan.

Still, this data highlights a major change in how countries choose their leaders: those chosen by blood and through violence have become rare, and those chosen by elections are far more common.

At the same time, elections alone don’t tell us anything about who gets to vote in them. That’s why we look at voting rights next.

# The expansion of voting rights

Two centuries ago, very few people could choose their country’s political leaders. It was mostly a privilege of the powerful.

As we just saw, elections became more common in the 19th century. But the right to vote in these elections remained heavily restricted: to men, to landowners or taxpayers, and to people of a certain skin color or religion.

Over time, most of those restrictions fell away. Legal barriers based on gender, income, and ethnicity have largely disappeared. Some others, especially those based on age, citizenship, and criminal convictions, have remained in place. But across most of the world, the right to vote has been extended to almost all adult citizens.

The next chart shows this spread of universal voting rights. Because the legal right to vote doesn’t matter much if your country never holds elections, the chart also considers whether countries elect their governments and parliaments in practice. 3

We see in the chart that some countries (such as France, Mexico, Switzerland, and Venezuela) broadened voting rights in the mid-1800s — but only for men.

It wasn’t until a half-century later that women in New Zealand gained the right to vote in 1893, making it the first country to have universal voting rights. You can track individual countries in this chart.

More data on voting rights

- [Countries that have universal voting rights This data focuses on the legal right to vote, not whether elections are being held in practice.](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/countries-that-have-universal-voting-rights)
- [Share of adult citizens who have the right to vote This data looks at the exact share of people who have formal voting rights.](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/suffrage)

Progress remained slow until the second half of the 20th century. But then it happened fast: at the end of World War II, fewer than two dozen countries had universal voting rights in practice. When the Cold War ended, that number had gone up to almost 150.

The chart also shows that this number has fallen recently. That’s not because any country restricted formal voting rights, but because some countries stopped having elected parliaments and governments altogether.

Taken together, this chart and the one before show that elections were not the only thing that spread across the world; so did the right to vote in them.

This brings us to the next building block of an electoral democracy: elections and voting rights aren’t effective if those in power don’t face meaningful competition. Exercising your right to vote means you can hold your leaders accountable. It means citizens have options to choose from, and to kick out if they do a bad job. That is why we turn next to electoral competition.

# The rise of competitive elections

The introduction of elections has not always meant real competition. In many places, results have often been a foregone conclusion.

In some elections, there is only one candidate on the ballot and no real political opposition. In others, incumbents face opposition but undermine the contest in other ways: intimidating voters, bribing officials to meddle with the ballots, or pressuring the media for favorable coverage.

Where this happens, governments rarely lose, even when they govern badly. One core function of elections — holding leaders accountable — is missing.

But over recent decades, many elections have become much more competitive: voters are now more likely to choose freely among several candidates, and fraud, if it happens at all, is less likely to change the result.

As a result, incumbents are more likely to lose power, which gives them reason to govern in ways voters actually want.

In the next chart, we track this through a proxy: we plot changes in electoral competition by looking at where elections recently led to a change in government (also called an electoral turnover). To do that, we adapted the data from the Lexical Index project. 4

The chart shows that competition for political office is a rarer and more recent development than elections and universal voting rights. (You can track individual countries in this chart.)

In the late 18th and early 19th centuries, elections very rarely led to a change in government.

There was some progress in the later 19th and early 20th centuries, as well as a wave of political competition after World War I, when at one point more than 30 countries had recently seen power change hands, especially in Europe. But that faded again in the wake of World War II.

After steady but limited progress between the 1950s and 1980s, changes in government spread rapidly in the 1990s, reaching more than half of all countries.

In the last two decades, political competition has increased more slowly. In 2025, 111 out of 199 countries had experienced a recent electoral turnover.

The chart shows that political competition, as captured by electoral turnovers, has become much more common. Voters often decide they’d like a change in who holds power, and as a result, political leaders have to work harder to win over voters.

This is by no means a perfect proxy. Electoral turnovers are more likely to happen under political competition, but the two are not the same.

Elections can be competitive without a change in government. Consider the case of Japan, where the Liberal Democratic Party has been in power almost continuously for the last 70 years, not because the party engaged in fraud or voter intimidation, but because it has remained popular and the opposition has been fragmented.

Similarly, turnovers can happen without competition. Incumbents can intimidate voters, stuff ballots, and persecute the media, and still lose. The loss doesn’t mean that the election was clean; it just means that it was clean enough for the opposition to squeak out a win.

Other measures of electoral competition

- [Competitive elections The Lexical Index’s own indicator of electoral competition.](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/competitive-elections-lexical)
- [Free and Fair Elections Index Expert-coded data of the degree of electoral competition.](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/free-and-fair-elections-index)

# How electoral democracies became the majority

In a democracy, we would expect governments and parliaments to be elected, almost all adults to be able to vote, and elections to be genuinely competitive. In the previous sections, we looked at these different building blocks separately. But we haven’t looked at when all of them come together.

So in the next chart, we track the countries that met all these conditions simultaneously. The Lexical Index project classifies countries as “electoral democracies” if they have an elected government and parliament, universal voting rights, a political opposition, and competitive elections. On the chart below, we call countries that don’t have all of these features “non-democracies”. 5

Until the late 19th century, no country met all the conditions of an electoral democracy. That changed in 1893, when women gained the right to vote in New Zealand, where elections had already become competitive.

Other countries followed, but progress was relatively slow. Democracies did not become a majority until the 1990s. By 2025, 117 countries qualified, against 82 that did not. You can see the breakdown in the small chart (click to enlarge).

 Click to explore

In the chart, we can also see that the spread of electoral democracies was uneven and marked by clear setbacks. The clearest expression of that is the 1930s: there were 20 democracies in the early years of the decade, but only nine remained by its end.

Another setback is visible more recently. In 2015, the number of countries that met all conditions reached its highest historical level, at 130 countries. The number has since decreased by 13, affecting countries from around the world, including Côte d’Ivoire, Nicaragua, and Serbia.
